'''Holders, rarity and distribution''' is the part of tokenomics that supply figures hide. A million coins is a million coins — but a million coins split twenty ways and a million coins split ten thousand ways are '''not the same asset''', and they will not behave the same in any market. This page is part of the series under [[How Cryptocurrencies Gain Value]].

== 1. The same supply, four different assets ==

Take exactly 1,000,000 coins and change nothing except how many people hold them.

* '''20 holders''' — 50,000 each. Each person owns '''5% of everything'''. Any one of them can end the market on a bad morning.
* '''500 holders''' — 2,000 each. Each owns '''0.2%'''.
* '''10,000 holders''' — 100 each. Each owns '''0.01%'''.
* '''100,000,000 holders''' — 0.01 each. No individual position is large — and the number of people a single price move now reaches is enormous. Which of those two facts dominates is the subject of §4.

The supply number is identical in all four. What changed is '''how rare a coin is from any one person's point of view''', and that is the thing that actually sets behaviour. At twenty holders a coin is common — the person next to you has fifty thousand. At ten thousand holders the same coin is rare: getting a hundred means finding someone willing to give up a hundred, and most of them are not.

This is the sense in which '''wide distribution manufactures scarcity without changing supply.''' You have not burned anything. You have made each unit harder to get hold of.

== 2. Why concentration is a price problem, not just a fairness problem ==

A concentrated holder base creates '''overhang''': a known quantity of coins that could hit the market, which every informed buyer prices in before bidding. The thinner the book (see [[Volume, Liquidity, and Depth]]), the worse this gets, because the overhang is enormous relative to the depth.

Research bears out that this is the normal state rather than the exception. One 2026 study found that ERC-20 Gini coefficients '''remain uniformly close to 1''' throughout the observation period — near-total inequality.<ref>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.24176</ref> Governance tokens can be worse: in one analysis of Compound, '''8 delegates''' could carry any governance action between them.<ref>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.01176</ref>

Two metrics are worth knowing:

* '''Gini coefficient''' — relative inequality, 0 (perfectly even) to 1 (one holder has everything).
* '''Nakamoto coefficient''' — the absolute '''count''' of entities needed to reach a control threshold. It answers "how many people would have to agree", which Gini cannot.<ref>https://bitquery.io/blog/wealth-distribution-in-token-economy</ref>

They can disagree, and that is informative: a high Gini with a high Nakamoto coefficient means wealth is uneven overall but '''the top is itself broad'''. Both need care — a liquidity pool, a burn address or a staking contract will show up as a giant "holder" and must be excluded before the numbers mean anything.<ref>https://bitquery.io/blog/wealth-distribution-in-token-economy</ref>

== 3. The arithmetic that actually funds a chain ==

Here is the part that changes what you build. Suppose each participant brings in '''$10''' of outside money — a genuinely small amount, the price of lunch.

* 20 people × $10 = '''$200'''
* 500 people × $10 = '''$5,000'''
* 10,000 people × $10 = '''$100,000'''
* 100,000 people × $10 = '''$1,000,000'''

Twenty people cannot fund a market by being generous. They can only fund it by being '''rich''', and money from twenty rich people is a different instrument: it arrives with expectations, it leaves in one decision, and while it is there it owns you.

Ten thousand people at ten dollars is the same hundred thousand dollars with '''none of those properties'''. No single exit matters. The bid is broad. And critically, those ten thousand people are not only capital — they are the holders in §1, the depth in [[Volume, Liquidity, and Depth]], and the users who create demand for whatever the coin is actually '''for''' ([[Utilities and Sinks]]).

This is why the growth strategy and the tokenomics are '''the same strategy'''. More holders is not a vanity metric; it is simultaneously more scarcity per person, more incoming value, more book depth and more utility demand.

=== Does the research support it? Metcalfe's law, and its honest exponent ===

The claim that more holders is worth more money is not just our argument — it is the most-tested quantitative claim in the field, and it comes out partly confirmed and partly cut down.

'''Metcalfe's law''' says a network's value grows with the '''square''' of its users, because value lives in the connections between them and n users have n(n-1)/2 possible pairs. Applied to crypto: Alabi found Bitcoin and Ethereum value moved in proportion to the square of unique daily users,<ref>https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0191886917301344</ref> and Peterson reported that '''over 70% of the variance''' in Bitcoin's value was explained by a Metcalfe-style model of network size.<ref>https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3078248</ref>

Then the cuts, which matter more than the confirmation:

* '''The exponent is not 2.''' Wheatley and co-authors fitting the relationship generally found an exponent of about '''1.69''', not 2 — still strongly super-linear, but materially weaker than the square — and used that fit to argue Bitcoin was significantly overvalued at the time.<ref>https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.05663</ref> A Goldman Sachs estimate landed near 1.9. The useful reading: value grows '''faster than linearly''' with participants. The exact power is unsettled and anyone quoting n² as a law is overselling it.
* '''Correlation is not causation.''' Users and price rise together in a bull market. The models cannot separate "more users made the price" from "a rising price attracted users".
* '''Full connectivity is a fiction.''' Metcalfe assumes everyone can transact with everyone and values all of it; in real networks each participant meaningfully connects to far fewer — on the order of n^(2/3) others. That is one reason the fitted exponent lands below 2.
* '''Active addresses are a bad proxy for people.''' One person runs several wallets, exchanges hold millions of users behind a handful of addresses, dormant wallets inflate holder counts, and layer-two activity never touches the base chain at all.

So the arithmetic in §3 stands — but it stands as '''super-linear growth with a contested exponent and a causation problem''', not as a formula that converts a holder count into a price. Combined with §4 below, the defensible version is narrow and still useful: '''participants who can be reached and activated raise the value of a network faster than their number suggests''' — and on a thin, responsive market, a small balance is no bar to being reached.

== 4. On a thin market, a small holder is not dust ==

An earlier revision of this page called holders of less than one token '''"dust"''' and said they "never return" and do not count. '''That was wrong''', and the reason it was wrong is the most useful thing on this page — because it is the same mechanism as [[Volume, Liquidity, and Depth]], read in the other direction.

Start with the raw numbers, which are real: of '''25,096''' VKBT holders, '''19,694 hold under one whole token'''; of '''15,039''' CURE holders, '''13,683''' do. Full detail in [[The STEEM HIVE BLURT MELEK VKBT and CURE Matrix|the Matrix]].

Now the four reasons the dismissive reading of those numbers does not hold:

# '''A thin market is a responsive market.''' It takes very little capital to move the price of a token this size — that is precisely what the depth figures say, including the CURE bid and ask that have stood '''2,700×''' apart. Thinness is usually discussed as a weakness, and on the exit side it is. On the '''entry''' side the same property means a modest bid produces a '''large percentage move'''.
# '''Every holder sees it.''' An engine wallet shows a balance and what that balance is worth. A large percentage move is therefore '''visible in all 25,096 wallets at once''', at no cost to anybody. The holder base is not an inert ledger entry — it is a '''distribution list for a price signal''', and the signal reaches everyone on it simultaneously.
# '''A visible move produces the one thing a thin token lacks.''' A holder who sees their balance move does one of two things: '''buys more, or sells some.''' Both are '''volume'''. Both are the second trade that §4 of [[Volume, Liquidity, and Depth]] identifies as the thing a shallow book needs in order to deepen. Somebody who can be activated by a price move is an '''economically live participant''', whatever their balance is today.
# '''Cheapness multiplies reach.''' The lower the price and the thinner the book, the '''more holders a given amount of buying can reach and activate'''. A large holder count and a small average balance is not a contradiction of §3's argument — it is §3's argument with the unit price moved.

So the correct reading is the opposite of the old one: '''a large holder base on a highly responsive market is an asset''', and the smallness of the individual balances does not cancel it. Nothing about holding 0.4 of a token prevents someone from noticing a 10× and acting on it.

=== What the numbers do and do not tell you ===

Keeping the part of the old paragraph that was actually defensible, and dropping the part that was not:

* '''A holder count does not tell you how much capital is behind a token.''' You cannot read a market cap, a floor or a dollar figure off a holder count. That is the one true caution, and it is a caution about '''arithmetic''', not about whether those holders matter.
* '''The counts further up the curve answer a different question''' — who holds '''size'''. VKBT has '''2,992''' holders of 10+, '''1,069''' of 100+ and '''207''' of 1,000+; CURE has '''438''' of 10+, '''64''' of 100+ and '''3''' of 1,000+. That is the number to look at for depth of commitment.
* '''Both are real information about different things.''' Breadth tells you how many people a move reaches. Size tells you who can move it. Neither makes the other irrelevant, and this wiki will quote both.
* '''How a base was acquired still matters for conviction''' — but that is a statement about acquisition, not a licence to discount anybody. Ours was '''purchased at market and given away through curation''' — earned by posting rather than sprayed at wallets. See the Matrix.

== 5. Float: the supply that is actually for sale ==

Supply is not the same as the amount that can be bought. The '''float''' is what is liquid and unlocked right now, and it is usually far smaller.

On CURE, '''71.2% of supply is staked''' — 51,594 of 72,440, summed from the `stake` field across all 15,776 balance rows — leaving a liquid float of roughly '''20,800 units'''. VKBT is '''41.9%''' staked (985,238 of 2,352,205). Re-derived 30 October 2026; note that `supply` minus `circulatingSupply` is '''not''' stake on Hive-Engine and gives an answer wrong by orders of magnitude. Staked coins are not on the market, so the float — not the supply — is what a buyer is competing for, and it is what a seller can actually dump.

A small float cuts both ways with total honesty: it means less overhang, and it means '''more violent price moves in both directions''', because any order is large relative to what is available. Anyone reading a small-float chart should know that the volatility is structural, not a signal.

== Not investment advice ==

This page explains distribution mechanics. It is '''not''' a claim that any token is undervalued, '''not''' a prediction, and '''not''' a suggestion to buy or sell. Small-float assets are structurally volatile; that is a description, not a recommendation.

== Coverage ==
Covers how identical supply behaves differently across holder counts, concentration as an overhang and price problem, the Gini and Nakamoto metrics with their caveats, the arithmetic of many small contributions versus few large ones, the correction of an earlier revision that dismissed sub-one-token holders as "dust" (a thin market is a responsive market, a move is visible in every wallet, and an activated holder supplies the volume the book needs), the distinction between breadth and size as separate information, and float versus supply. Holder and stake figures are carried from the Matrix pages; treat them as of their capture dates. Gives no valuation verdicts.

The Metcalfe's-law subsection reviews the quantitative research on network value (Alabi 2017, Peterson 2018, Wheatley et al. 2018) and states its limits: a fitted exponent near 1.69 rather than 2, unresolved causation, the full-connectivity assumption, and active addresses as a poor proxy for people.
